questions.question: A seller has private information (her type, such as quality) that affects a buyer's value of trading. Adverse selection requires one more feature of the trade. Which one?
options: The buyer is more risk-averse than the seller
The seller's action after the sale is hidden from the buyer
Both parties' values for the good are equal for every type
The price or contract terms cannot depend on the seller's type

questions.question: An insurer cannot observe customers' characteristics. Which situation is adverse selection rather than moral hazard?
options: Customers drive less carefully once they are insured
Insured workers put in less effort because effort is unobserved
Customers already know their own accident risk when they buy
Customers stop locking their bicycles after buying theft cover

questions.question: In a trade with privately informed sellers, the uninformed buyer's price offer and the sellers' type-contingent acceptance rules form a Bayesian Nash equilibrium in which some mutually beneficial trades do not occur. Why do these trades fail?
options: Because some players make irrational choices given their information
Because each player best responds, and the price draws mainly bad types
Because the buyer does not know the probability distribution of types
Because Bayesian Nash equilibria never produce efficient outcomes

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 8 and $L$ at 2, a buyer values them at 11 and 3. The buyer offers a price $p$; each seller type accepts iff $p$ is at least her own value. If she offers $p=8$, what are her expected value of the good she obtains and her expected payoff?
options: Value $11$, payoff $3$
Value $3$, payoff $-5$
Value $5$, payoff $-3$
Value $7$, payoff $-1$

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 8 and $L$ at 2, a buyer values them at 11 and 3. The buyer offers a price $p$; each seller type accepts iff $p$ is at least her own value. Suppose she offers the low price $p=2$. Which seller types accept, and what is her expected payoff?
options: Only $L$; payoff $1$
Both types; payoff $5$
Only $L$; payoff $\tfrac{1}{2}$
Neither type; payoff $0$

questions.question: A firm can offer only one wage to all job applicants, and applicants differ in what they are worth to the firm. In which situation does adverse selection arise?
options: Applicants know their own productivity, and mostly the least productive accept
Productivity is public, so the firm hires only applicants worth the wage
Hired workers shirk because the firm cannot observe their effort
All applicants are equally productive, so every acceptor is equally good

questions.question: In a used-good market with private quality, the buyer's best offer is accepted only by low-quality sellers, although each high-quality good is worth more to the buyer than to its seller. Why is this outcome not Pareto efficient?
options: Because the low-quality sellers receive less than their value
Because trades of high-quality goods with positive gains do not happen
Because the buyer earns a negative expected payoff in equilibrium
Because Pareto efficiency requires every type to receive the same price

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\mu$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 8 and $L$ at 2, a buyer values them at 11 and 3. The buyer offers a price $p$; each seller type accepts iff $p$ is at least her own value. The buyer compares $p=8$ (both types accept) with $p=2$ (only $L$ accepts). For which $\mu$ is $p=8$ at least as good for her?
options: $\mu\ge\tfrac{5}{8}$
$\mu\ge\tfrac{3}{4}$
$\mu\ge\tfrac{2}{3}$
$\mu\ge\tfrac{1}{3}$

questions.question: A seller's quality is low, medium or high with probability $\tfrac{1}{3}$ each; she values it at 2, 5 or 8, the buyer at 3, 6 or 9. The buyer offers $p$, accepted by each type iff $p$ is at least her value. Which qualities trade at the buyer's best offer?
options: All three, at $p=8$
Low and medium, at $p=5$
Only high, at $p=8$
Only low, at $p=2$

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\tfrac{1}{4}$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 6 and $L$ at 1, a buyer values them at 9 and 2. A free inspection now reveals the quality to the buyer, who makes a take-it-or-leave-it offer for that quality; each type accepts iff the offer is at least her value. What is the buyer's expected payoff?
Sellers have private costs of producing a standard good whose value to every buyer is the same, whatever the seller's cost. A buyer posts one price. Does adverse selection arise?
options: Yes, since low-cost sellers accept lower prices than high-cost ones
Yes, since any private information leads to adverse selection
No, since the private type does not affect the buyer's value
No, since the buyer can always offer a price no seller rejects

questions.question: In a market with privately informed sellers whose quality matters to buyers, what does the word "adverse" in adverse selection refer to?
options: Those who accept are disproportionately the types worst for the offer-maker
The informed side deliberately lies about its type to the uninformed side
The uninformed side selects the worst types on purpose to pay less
Prices are always set below every type's value, which is adverse for sellers

questions.question: A buyer makes a take-it-or-leave-it price offer to a seller whose quality type $\theta\in\{L,H\}$ is private. In the Bayesian Nash equilibrium of this game, what is the seller's strategy?
options: A rule giving, for each type, whether to accept each possible price
A single decision to accept or reject, chosen before learning her type
The price she would ask if she could make the offer herself
Her expected value of the good, averaged over both types

questions.question: A seller privately knows if her good is of high quality $H$ (probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$) or low quality $L$; she values $H$ at 8 and $L$ at 2, a buyer values them at 11 and 3. The buyer offers a price $p$; each seller type accepts iff $p$ is at least her own value. A buyer reasons: "the average good is worth 7 to me, so offering 6 gives me $7-6=1$." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: At $p=6$ only $L$ sellers accept, so the relevant value is 3
She should compare 7 with the average seller value 5
The average must weight $H$ more heavily since it is worth more
At $p=6$ only $H$ sellers accept, so the value is 11

questions.question: A seller's type $t$ is uniform on $[0,1]$; she values her good at $t$ and the buyer at $1.5t$, so every trade with $t>0$ has positive gains. The buyer offers a price $p\in(0,1]$, which the seller accepts iff $t\le p$. As a function of $p$, what is the buyer's expected value of the good conditional on acceptance?
options: $\tfrac{p}{2}$

questions.question: An insurer faces 70% low-risk customers (expected loss 10, willing to pay at most 18) and 30% high-risk customers (expected loss 40, willing to pay at most 50). It must charge every buyer the same premium, equal to the expected claim per insured customer. Who ends up insured, and at what premium?
options: Both groups, at $19$, which is below the high-risk limit of $50$
Only high risks, at $40$, since pooling needs $19>18$
Both groups, at $25$, the equal-weight average of the two expected losses
Only low risks, at $10$, since they form the majority of customers
